title: Retention and Resilience: How to Keep Your Best Prison Officers in the Job November 17, 2026
author: Unlocked Graduates
summary: Unlocked Graduates explains how its graduate scheme raised two-year frontline retention of prison officers to 78.9 percent against 60.8 percent for a comparison group, an 18 point gap. The core claim is that retention should be managed on purpose rather than left to chance. The team maps the predictable emotional highs and lows of the first two years and acts ahead of the lows, for example by preparing recruits for a Christmas dip, sending a care package before first night shifts and writing to staff after an assault. Independent research on alumni found the quality of the line manager is the biggest retention factor, yet only 51 percent rate their line manager's support as good compared with 94 percent for their mentor. Accountability loops such as weekly red, amber and green tracking and a toolkit of rehearsed retention conversations make retention a named job. The piece also defines resilience as engaging with support, not tolerating trauma.
points: Make retention an explicit job for line managers, with accountability, tracking and training, and change the belief that leavers are inevitable.
Map the predictable low points of the early service journey and intervene before they arrive.
Line manager quality is the largest single driver of retention, so invest in the skills and capacity of that role.
Select for resilience that seeks support, and teach protective routines as a professional responsibility.
Recruitment and preparation come first, since retention only pays off when well chosen, well prepared people are kept.
quotes: People rarely leave over one thing. They leave when the lows come and nobody has prepared them, noticed, or taken responsibility for helping them stay.
After two years, 78.9% of Unlocked participants were still operational on the frontline, compared with 60.8% of the comparison group.
If you respond to the predictable lows in advance, you have a much better chance of keeping people.
The research found that the biggest factor in retention among Unlocked alumni is the quality of their line manager.

Many have too many officers to line manage to really commit to this, and many more have simply never been given the skills, tools or training to retain good staff. As a result, retention is too often left to chance rather than managed on purpose.

In our experience, resilient people are not those who are comfortable in unpleasant or traumatic situations. They are people who know how to protect themselves in those environments, by actively engaging with support.
The aim is to shift their locus of control, the sense of what is within their power, from resignation towards action.
